sections.body: This section covers the practical side of using artificial intelligence for quantitative research and reproducible workflows. AI is now used to draft and debug statistical code, translate plain language questions into database queries, and help package notebooks so others can rerun an analysis. It can also simulate a study design before any data is collected, showing where a planned test might lack power or produce ambiguous results. These are not hypothetical capabilities; they appear in working notebooks, code assistants, and research pipelines that handle real datasets.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The work is uneven. Reproducible notebooks and pipelines are well supported by AI tools that can document dependencies, freeze environments, and generate setup files, but they still require a human to verify that the output matches the original analysis. Asking data questions in plain language works for simple aggregations and filters, yet it often fails when a question involves nested logic, missing data, or domain specific definitions. Large-scale compute on institutional data is possible, but the honest limits are cost, data governance, and the risk that a generated query touches records it should not. Statistical code generation is reliable for standard tests and plots, less so for custom models or edge cases. Testing a study design before data collection is promising, but simulations are only as good as the assumptions a researcher puts into them.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader who wants to make their own work rerunnable would start with Reproducible Notebooks and Pipelines, which shows how AI helps package code, data, and environment details. Asking Data Questions in Plain Language is the page for turning a vague research question into a concrete query or analysis plan without writing SQL or Python first. Large-Scale Compute on Institutional Data covers the harder case of running analyses across sensitive or very large datasets, where AI assists with orchestration and compliance checks. Writing Statistical Code with AI is the reference for generating, checking, and correcting R or Python code for statistics. Testing a Study Design Before Data Collection explains how AI can simulate a planned experiment or survey, so a researcher can spot weak designs before spending time and money on real data.
